rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'A subclass declaration' does not say the subclass method is static, and the JLS calls an instance method with that signature overriding (a compile-time error). The rewrite names both methods as static.
rewrite.statement: A subclass static method with the same signature as a superclass static method overrides it.
rewrite.explanation: The subclass method hides the superclass one: a call through a superclass-typed reference still runs the superclass's static method, because the compile-time type picks a class method.
rewrite.misconception: Static methods participate in overriding like instance methods.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'an inherited public instance method with a body' also covers a default inherited from a second interface, which causes a compile-time error rather than winning. The rewrite names the superclass as the origin. Confirmed by JLS 8.4.8: a default is not inherited when 'No concrete method inherited by C from its direct superclass type has a signature that is a subsignature'.
rewrite.statement: A public concrete instance method inherited from a class's superclass wins over a matching interface default.
rewrite.explanation: A class does not inherit an interface default when a concrete method inherited from its superclass already has a matching signature, so the superclass method is the one that runs.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: no Java SE 25 page supports the return-type case. JLS 6.5.5.1 forbids a type parameter in a static context, and JLS 8.1.3 defines static context only for statements, declarations and expressions, not method headers; JLS 8.1.2 only points back to 6.5.5.1. The rewrite tests the case 6.5.5.1 states ('must not appear in the body of a static method declared by C'), keeping the answer false.
rewrite.statement: Inside a static method of `class Box<T>`, a local variable can be declared with the type `T`.
rewrite.explanation: A class's type parameter may not be named in a static context such as a static method body, where no current instance exists, so a local variable of type T there is a compile-time error.
rewrite.misconception: Static methods of a generic class have access to the class's type parameter.

rewrite.statement: `class A{void f(Object x){}} class B extends A{@Override void f(String x){}}` compiles.
rewrite.explanation: The subclass's f(String) overloads f(Object), so @Override makes this declaration a compile-time error.
rewrite.misconception: @Override accepts an overload with a different parameter type.

rewrite.reason: tell: removes 'accepts' (false-only permission verb) and balances 'compiles' toward false. Same fact and answer (false); JLS 9.4.1.2 confirmed.

rewrite.reason: tell: removes 'accepts' (false-only permission verb); the hedge 'may' was balanced 2T/2F. Same fact and answer (false); JLS 8.9.2 confirmed.

cards.statement: A subclass static method with the same signature as a superclass static method overrides it.
cards.explanation: The subclass method hides the superclass one: a call through a superclass-typed reference still runs the superclass's static method, because the compile-time type picks a class method.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. JLS 25 §8.4.8.2 confirmed: 'If a class C declares or inherits a static method m, then m is said to hide any method m'...'. Example 8.4.8.2-1: Super s = new Sub(); s.greeting() 'uses the type of s, namely Super, to figure out, at compile time, which class method to invoke'.

cards.statement: A public concrete instance method inherited from a class's superclass wins over a matching interface default.
cards.explanation: A class does not inherit an interface default when a concrete method inherited from its superclass already has a matching signature, so the superclass method is the one that runs.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. JLS 25 §8.4.8 confirmed: a default m is inherited only if 'No concrete method inherited by C from its direct superclass type has a signature that is a subsignature of the signature of m as a member of D'. §8.4.8.1 lets an inherited public mC override mA, so naming the method public avoids the access error.

cards.statement: Inside a static method of `class Box<T>`, a local variable can be declared with the class's type parameter `T`.
cards.explanation: A class's type parameter may not be named in a static context such as a static method body, where no current instance exists, so a local variable of type T there is a compile-time error.
cards.reason: Both lenses gave the same fix. 'the type `T`' could mean the static method's own type parameter (`static <T> void m(){ T x; }` compiles), so the statement now names the class's type parameter. JLS 25 §6.5.5.1 confirmed: 'The type name does not occur in a static context (§8.1.3)... the type name must not appear in the body of a static method declared by C'. Statement is about 107 characters.

cards.explanation: Integer.equals requires its argument to be an Integer holding the same int value. A Long argument yields false.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Integer Javadoc (Java SE 25) confirmed: 'The result is true if and only if the argument is not null and is an Integer object that contains the same int value as this object.'

cards.statement: `class A{void f(Object x){}} class B extends A{@Override void f(String x){}}` compiles.
cards.explanation: The subclass's f(String) overloads f(Object), so @Override makes this declaration a compile-time error.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. JLS 25 §9.6.4.4 confirmed: when a method is annotated with @Override, one of three conditions must hold 'or a compile-time error occurs'. f(String) does not override f(Object), it is not override-equivalent to an Object method, and B is not a record.

cards.statement: An interface declaring `default String toString() { return "x"; }` compiles.
cards.explanation: An interface's default toString implementation produces a compile-time error because it matches a non-private Object method.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. JLS 25 §9.4.1.2 confirmed: 'It is a compile-time error if a default method is override-equivalent (§8.4.2) with a non-private method of the class Object'.

cards.statement: An enum class may declare its constructor with the `protected` access modifier.
cards.explanation: Java rejects protected enum constructors at compile time. Enum constructors use private access, explicitly or implicitly.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. JLS 25 §8.9.2 confirmed: 'It is a compile-time error if a constructor declaration in an enum declaration is public or protected' and 'a constructor declaration with no access modifiers is private'.

cards.statement: A `List<Integer>` value is assignable to a variable of type `List<Number>`.
cards.explanation: Java rejects assigning a List<Integer> to a List<Number> variable. A subtype relationship between element classes does not transfer to these parameterized types.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. JLS 25 §4.10.2 confirmed: the direct supertypes of C<T1,...,Tn> include 'C<S1,...,Sn>, where Si contains Ti (§4.5.1)'. A non-wildcard type argument contains only itself, so List<Number> is not a supertype of List<Integer>.
